docs.title: quantbench ⚖️
docs.text: A unified, first-principles quantization engine, bit-packing runtime, 2:4 sparsity toolkit, and Quality-vs-Speed Pareto evaluation benchmark in pure Python and PyTorch.

docs.title: Why quantbench?
docs.text:
Most developers treat LLM quantization as a black box: they download GGUF or AWQ checkpoints without knowing how scales and zero-points are calculated, how 4-bit signed integers are packed into memory bytes, or why activation outliers in attention layers cause naive INT8 quantization to collapse.

quantbench implements these algorithms from scratch with radical transparency and zero compiled C++/CUDA dependencies, and provides a benchmark CLI that measures empirical perplexity degradation alongside generation throughput.

docs.title: 📦 Quick Installation
docs.text:
Install directly from PyPI:

pip install quantbench-engine

# Or via uv
uv add quantbench-engine

docs.title: 🚀 Navigation
docs.text:
• Mathematical Foundations — Zero-preserving affine invariants, symmetric AbsMax, blockwise grouping, and OCP FP8 emulation.
  • Sub-Byte Bit-Packing — INT4 nibble packing, two's complement sign extension, and BitNet 1.58b ternary vectorization.
  • 2:4 Structured Sparsity — NVIDIA Ampere/Ada/Hopper sparse tensor core layout and metadata encoding.
  • Advanced Calibration — SmoothQuant channel migration, AWQ Frobenius grid search, and GPTQ second-order Hessian updates.
  • Drop-in QuantLinear Layers — Replacing PyTorch nn.Linear with compressed sub-byte persistent buffers.
  • Pareto Evaluation — Layer SQNR (dB), sliding-window perplexity on WikiText-2/C4, and terminal Pareto curves.

docs.title: Sub-Byte Bit-Packing Runtimes
docs.text: Standard CPU and GPU memory controllers address memory in 8-bit bytes. Storing 4-bit, 2-bit, or ternary weights requires bit-manipulation packing routines.

docs.title: 1. INT4 Nibble Packing (int4_pack.py)
docs.text:
Two 4-bit nibbles are packed into each uint8 byte container:

\[\text{byte} = (v_0 \ \& \ \text{0x0F}) \mid ((v_1 \ \& \ \text{0x0F}) \ll 4)\] 
Byte: [ b7 b6 b5 b4 | b3 b2 b1 b0 ]
         Value 1         Value 0
       (High Nibble)   (Low Nibble)

docs.title: Sign Extension in Two's Complement
docs.text:
Signed 4-bit values span \([-8, 7]\). When extracting the high nibble via arithmetic shift (byte >> 4), hardware handles sign propagation automatically. When extracting the low nibble:

\[v_{\text{signed}} = (v_{\text{raw}} \ge 8) \ ? \ (v_{\text{raw}} - 16) : v_{\text{raw}}\]

quantbench implements vectorized PyTorch tensor bit-shifts with zero CPU Python loops.

docs.title: 2. BitNet 1.58b Ternary Packing (ternary_pack.py)
docs.text: BitNet weights belong to \(\{-1, 0, +1\}\).

docs.title: Hardware-Friendly 2-Bit SIMD Packing
docs.text:
Maps ternary values to unsigned offset integers: $\(u = v + 1 \in \{0, 1, 2\}\)$

Four weights are packed into one byte: $\(\text{byte} = u_0 \mid (u_1 \ll 2) \mid (u_2 \ll 4) \mid (u_3 \ll 6)\)$ Achieves \(8\times\) compression over FP16 with fast bitwise parallel dequantization.

docs.title: Base-3 Radix Packing
docs.text: Because \(3^5 = 243 \le 255\), five ternary values can theoretically fit into a single byte: $\(\text{byte} = \sum_{i=0}^4 u_i \cdot 3^i\)$ Achieves theoretical maximal density (\(\log_2(3) \approx 1.585\) bits per weight).

docs.title: Advanced Calibration Algorithms
docs.text: When quantizing large language models to 4 bits or 8 bits, naive rounding degrades generation quality. quantbench implements the three leading post-training calibration techniques from scratch.

docs.title: 1. SmoothQuant Outlier Migration
docs.text:
LLM activations display extreme channel outliers (up to \(100\times\) larger than normal channels), causing INT8 activation quantization to clip or collapse resolution.

SmoothQuant migrates dynamic range from difficult activations \(X\) to easy-to-quantize weights \(W\) using a per-channel scaling vector \(s\):

\[Y = (X \cdot \text{diag}(s)^{-1}) \cdot (\text{diag}(s) \cdot W)\]

Where migration scale \(s_j\) is given by: $\(s_j = \frac{\max(|X_j|)^\alpha}{\max(|W_j|)^{1 - \alpha}}\)$

The scaling factor \(s\) is absorbed directly into the preceding LayerNorm or RMSNorm weights, leaving runtime matrix multiplication intact.

docs.title: 2. Activation-Aware Weight Quantization (AWQ)
docs.text:
AWQ observes that not all weights are equally important: only the top \(1\%\text{--}2\%\) of weights corresponding to large activation magnitudes govern model perplexity.

Rather than quantizing salient weights into separate FP16 layers, AWQ applies a per-channel protection scale \(s\):

\[W' = W \cdot \text{diag}(s)\]

Optimal scale \(\alpha \in [0, 1]\) is discovered via fast grid search on calibration tokens to minimize Frobenius reconstruction error:

\[\min_\alpha \| W X - \text{dequantize}(\text{quantize}(W \cdot \text{diag}(s))) \cdot \text{diag}(s)^{-1} X \|_F^2\]

docs.title: 3. GPTQ Second-Order Hessian Updates
docs.text:
GPTQ frames quantization as an Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS) error compensation problem using second-order Taylor expansion:

\[E \approx \frac{1}{2} (w - \hat{w})^T H (w - \hat{w}), \quad H = 2 X X^T\]
  1. Cholesky Inversion: Inverts the damped Hessian \(H_{\text{damp}} = H + \lambda \cdot \text{mean}(\text{diag}(H)) \cdot I\) using Cholesky decomposition \(H = L L^T\).
  2. Sequential Greedy Rounding: When quantizing column \(q\), downstream remaining columns \(F\) are updated: $\(\Delta W_{:, F} = - \frac{W_{:, q} - \hat{W}_{:, q}}{[H^{-1}]_{qq}} \cdot [H^{-1}]_{q, F}\)$
  3. Block Updates: Accumulates errors across blocks (e.g. 128 columns) and updates remaining weights using single dense GEMMs.

docs.title: Mathematical Foundations of Quantization
docs.text: Quantization projects continuous floating-point tensors into discrete low-bit integer or floating-point representations.

docs.title: 1. Affine Asymmetric Quantization
docs.text:
Maps floating-point interval \([x_{\min}, x_{\max}]\) to integer grid \([q_{\min}, q_{\max}]\):

\[s = \frac{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}{2^b - 1}\] \[z = \text{round}\left(-\frac{x_{\min}}{s}\right) + q_{\min}\] \[q = \text{clamp}\left(\text{round}\left(\frac{x}{s}\right) + z, \; q_{\min}, \; q_{\max}\right)\]

Dequantization reconstructs the real value:

\[\hat{x} = (q - z) \cdot s\]

docs.title: The Zero-Preserving Invariant
docs.text:
If a tensor is purely positive (e.g. ReLU activations in \([0.5, 12.0]\)), a naive min-max scaling causes integer zero to represent a non-zero float. To preserve exact real-world zero:

\[x_{\min} = \min(x_{\min}, 0.0), \quad x_{\max} = \max(x_{\max}, 0.0)\]

This guarantees that zero-padding tokens and causal attention masks dequantize to exact \(0.0\), preventing bias injection into transformer hidden states.

docs.title: 2. Symmetric AbsMax Quantization
docs.text:
Centers the dynamic range at zero (\(z = 0\)), eliminating per-element subtraction during hardware matrix multiplication:

\[s = \frac{\max(|x|)}{2^{b-1} - 1}\] \[q = \text{clamp}\left(\text{round}\left(\frac{x}{s}\right), \; -(2^{b-1}), \; 2^{b-1}-1\right)\] \[\hat{x} = q \cdot s\]

docs.title: 3. Block-Wise (Group-Wise) Quantization
docs.text:
Per-tensor quantization uses a single scale \(s\) for an entire weight matrix. A single outlier forces \(s\) to expand, destroying the resolution of normal channels.

Block-wise quantization slices the matrix into independent groups of size \(G \in \{32, 64, 128\}\): * Each block computes an independent scale \(s_k\) and zero-point \(z_k\). * For \(G = 128\), scale metadata adds only \(16 / 128 = 0.125\) bits per weight, providing near-FP16 fidelity with INT4 weights.

docs.title: 4. OCP FP8 Formats (E4M3FN vs E5M2)
docs.text:
quantbench implements bit-exact software emulation of Open Compute Project (OCP) 8-bit floats:

Format Bit Layout Exponent Bias Max Finite Value Primary Use Case E4M3FN 1 sign, 4 exp, 3 mantissa 7 448.0 GEMM weights and activations (high precision) E5M2 1 sign, 5 exp, 2 mantissa 15 57344.0 Gradients and attention KV-caches (wide dynamic range)

docs.title: Quality vs Speed Pareto Evaluation
docs.text: Quantization always involves a trade-off between model quality (perplexity / SQNR) and generation throughput (memory compression / latency).

docs.title: Signal-to-Quantization-Noise Ratio (SQNR)
docs.text:
Measures reconstruction fidelity across layers in decibels (dB):

\[\text{SQNR (dB)} = 10 \cdot \log_{10} \left( \frac{\sum |W|^2}{\sum |W - \hat{W}|^2 + \epsilon} \right)\]
  • \(> 30\text{ dB}\): High fidelity (lossless or near-lossless generation).
  • \(20\text{--}30\text{ dB}\): Good fidelity (acceptable for production serving).
  • \(< 15\text{ dB}\): Noticeable degradation; requires calibration tuning (AWQ / GPTQ).

docs.title: Sliding-Window Perplexity
docs.text: Evaluates perplexity on WikiText-2 or C4 validation splits using sliding window stride \(S < L\) to ensure every token has preceding causal context.

docs.title: 2. Running Pareto Sweeps
docs.text:
Run the benchmark CLI to evaluate compression vs accuracy and render a terminal Pareto frontier:

quantbench pareto --formats fp16,int8,int4,ternary,sparse24

docs.title: Drop-in Neural Layers (QuantLinear)
docs.text:
In standard PyTorch, layers use torch.nn.Parameter, which forces 16-bit or 32-bit floats and tracks gradients.

QuantLinear (quantbench.nn.quant_linear) is a drop-in replacement for torch.nn.Linear that stores quantized weights directly inside sub-byte uint8 persistent buffers (register_buffer).

docs.title: 1. Supported Formats
docs.text:
• INT4 Groupwise: Group sizes \(G \in \{32, 64, 128\}\) with 4-bit nibbles packed into uint8 arrays.
  • INT8 AbsMax: Per-channel or per-tensor scales.
  • BitNet Ternary: Biased 2-bit offset packing (\(8\times\) compression).
  • Ampere 2:4 Structured Sparsity: Compressed values + 4-bit column index nibbles.

docs.title: 2. Dynamic Forward Execution
docs.text:
During the forward pass, QuantLinear unpacks integer weights directly in memory and scales them dynamically:

from quantbench.nn.quant_linear import QuantLinear
import torch.nn as nn

# Convert standard linear layer to INT4 blockwise (group size = 64)
linear = nn.Linear(1024, 4096)
quant_layer = QuantLinear.from_float(linear, format="int4", group_size=64)

# Forward pass with identical input dimensions
out = quant_layer(x)

docs.title: 3. Recursive Model Converter
docs.text:
Automatically replaces all nn.Linear layers across a Hugging Face model while excluding sensitive layers (such as the vocabulary lm_head):

from quantbench.nn.model_convert import convert_model_to_quant

model = convert_model_to_quant(model, format="int4", group_size=128, exclude_modules=["lm_head"])

docs.title: NVIDIA 2:4 Structured Sparsity (sparse_pack.py)
docs.text: NVIDIA Ampere, Ada Lovelace, and Hopper architectures support hardware-accelerated 2:4 structured sparsity.

docs.title: 1. The Hardware Invariant
docs.text:
For every block of 4 consecutive values along a matrix row, exactly 2 values must be zero (50% sparsity).

Dense 4-element block:   [ 0.0,  3.5,  0.0, -1.2 ]
Retained non-zero values: [ 3.5, -1.2 ]  (Column indices: 1 and 3)
2-bit column metadata:   idx0 = 1 (0b01), idx1 = 3 (0b11)
Metadata nibble:         (0b01 & 0x03) | ((0b11 & 0x03) << 2) = 0b1101 (13 decimal)

docs.title: 2. Memory & Math Acceleration
docs.text:
1. Storage Reduction: Retained non-zero weights form a compressed dense matrix of shape \((M, N/2)\) — slashing memory traffic by 50%.
  2. Metadata Layout: Two 2-bit indices form a 4-bit nibble per 4 elements. Eight matrix columns produce one 8-bit metadata byte.
  3. Sparse Tensor Cores: Hardware skips zero multiply-accumulate operations, doubling theoretical peak TFLOPS (\(2.0\times\) speedup).
